Geometric Series in a Square

Infinite SeriesFractionsLimits
Game: A square is cut into smaller and smaller pieces, and some are coloured. Watch how much of the square gets coloured in the end.
How to play: Press + to cut once more. Pick 2, 3 or 4 to see three different ways of cutting.

N 1
Show
Look for the math

Three proofs without words of sums of geometric series:

1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … = 1
1/3 + 1/9 + 1/27 + … = 1/2
1/4 + 1/16 + 1/64 + … = 1/3

Halves: the whole square

Shade half the square, then half of what is left, then half of that. Every step shades half of the white part, so the white part after k steps is 1/2k and the shaded part is 1 − 1/2k. Nothing white is safe for ever: the shading fills the square. (This picture is Warren Page's.)

Thirds: half the square

Cut the square into 3 × 3 and shade the three cells below the diagonal: 3/9 = 1/3. Then do the same in each of the three cells on the diagonal: 3 × 3/81 = 1/9, and so on. The cells above the diagonal are a mirror copy of the shaded ones, and between them they use up everything, since the diagonal cells shrink away. So the shaded part tends to exactly half.

Quarters: a third of the square

Cut into quarters and shade one; leave two more white, and cut the fourth again (Sunday A. Ajose's picture). At every size there are three equal quarters, one shaded and two white, so the shaded part is a third of everything except the shrinking corner: it tends to 1/3.

The formula

With ratio r, r + r² + … + rk = r(1 − rk)/(1 − r), which tends to r/(1 − r): 1, 1/2 and 1/3 for r = 1/2, 1/3, 1/4. The logic test checked, for every N the applet allows, that the coloured area is exactly the partial sum, that the coloured pieces never overlap, and (in exact whole-number arithmetic) that each partial sum falls short of its limit by 1/((q−1)qk).

Pick 4 and press + a few times. Can you see the same L-shape of three quarters at every size?
